--- Transcript body (timestamps approximate, transcription contains occasional errors) ---
[00:00] Samir: hey everyone thanks for joining, can you hear me okay?
[00:04] Marta: yes loud and clear, thanks Samir. we've got about 50 minutes, wanted to dig into observability for the private deployment and make sure we can see token-level traces end-to-end.
[00:12] Samir: perfect, Ivy will do most of the heavy lifting on the technical bits. quick intros?
[00:15] Ivy: hey hi, Ivy Chen, SE on runtime/observability. I've instrumented a few customers with OTEL and Grafana dashboards for token metrics.
[00:20] Priya: Priya, CTO, I'm mostly listening for architecture + compliance.
[00:23] Daniel: Daniel, SRE. we maintain Lyra's infra and Grafana stack. main asks: low-overhead traces, no PII leakage, and ability to correlate tokens to request ids for quality debugging.
[00:32] Ivy: great, that's exactly what we want to validate. quick agenda: OTEL collector placement in VPC, what to instrument (spans & token metrics), KV cache visibility, batching knobs, quantization profiling, and finally dashboard examples and alerts.
[00:44] Marta: sounds good. our current infra is EKS in a private VPC with private subnets; we run an internal OTEL collector cluster. we can't open internet egress for data plane.
[00:52] Samir: that's common — Redwood Private supports collector-sidecar or central collector in VPC, we can talk through both. Ivy, maybe start with how token-level metrics are emitted?
[00:59] Ivy: sure. at request time the runtime emits per-token counters and optional spans. token-level metrics include token_count, per-token-latency (ms), kv_cache_hit boolean per token, and model_variant used. Practically we expose them via OTEL as metrics and traces
[01:14] Ivy: the key is to avoid emitting a trace per token by default — that would be too high cardinality. instead we recommend composing a request-span that has token-level metrics as metrics arrays or bounded summaries. so you'd have a request span with attributes like token_count, p50_token_ms, p95_token_ms and an aggregated kv_cache_hit_ratio.
[01:34] Daniel: ok so we won't be shipping gigabytes of spans, but still want per-token forensic when debugging e.g., when KV cache misses spike. how do we get the raw token events on-demand?
[01:42] Ivy: good question — we support a sampling mode. default telemetry is aggregated at request granularity. for debug sessions you can enable high-fidelity tracing on a percentage of requests or with request tags (trace=true) so that the runtime exports a token-span list for those requests only. that keeps steady-state cardinality low.
[02:01] Marta: how do we control that from within our VPC? we don't want the runtime to egress traces externally.
[02:06] Samir: you can point the runtime to your internal OTEL collector endpoint over a VPC private link — Redwood Private will talk over the private network to your collector. no external egress required. the control plane (optional) can be separated, but data plane traces and logs stay in your VPC.
[02:24] Priya: what about encryption / KMS? we need to ensure token payloads are not written in plaintext to logs or traces.
[02:30] Ivy: by default we scrub token text from telemetry; traces include token indices, hashes, and length attributes, but not raw token surfaces. for on-demand debug traces you can opt-in to include raw tokens but we recommend HSM/KMS usage and short retention.
[02:43] Daniel: ok good. next, KV cache metrics — we need to see hit/miss per prefix and eviction rates. can Redwood expose per-shard cache counters?
[02:52] Ivy: yes, runtime exposes cache_shard_hit and cache_shard_miss counters, plus per-prefix stats if you set prefix_reporting=true. note that per-prefix reporting increases cardinality — we recommend predefining a small set of prefixes (e.g., prompt templates or top N user ids) for which you'll get fine-grained metrics.
[03:12] Marta: we have ~200 prompt templates, would that be too many?
[03:16] Ivy: 200 is on the high side for per-prefix metric labels. better to sample the top 20 and aggregate the rest. alternatively you can stream raw cache events into a separate low-cost collector for offline analysis.
[03:28] Daniel: how is the KV cache instrumented for quantized models? are evictions or misses more common after 4-bit quantization?
[03:35] Ivy: quantization mainly affects compute throughput and memory footprint. with int4 you can fit more KV cache in GPU memory, so misses can actually drop because more context can stay cached. however decoding latency per token may increase a small amount if kernel paths are different. we recommend benchmarking both with our quant profiles.
[03:51] Samir: quick fallback note — our runtime can route to a float32 variant if quantized performance causes quality regressions; that's part of routing policies.
[03:58] Priya: good. on batching: we run bursty traffic and want to understand p95/p99 tails. how does batching interact with latency SLOs?
[04:06] Ivy: batching reduces cost and increases throughput but adds scheduling delay. our scheduler supports latency targets per route; you can set max_wait_ms and max_batch_tokens. for low-latency routes we use smaller max_wait and lower batch size; for background embedding routes we allow large batches. We also have a predictive scheduler that uses recent inter-arrival times to decide whether to wait for more tokens.
[04:33] Daniel: is that predictive scheduler visible in telemetry? can we see when requests were held waiting for batching?
[04:38] Ivy: yes — there's a batching_delay_ms metric and a batch_size gauge exported per route. also spans contain batch_id and wait_before_dispatch_ms so you can correlate p99 latency spikes to batching decisions.
[04:52] Marta: that will help tune our routing. question: we'd like to draw a single Grafana dashboard that shows top N routes, p95 request latency, p95 token latency, KV hit rate, and batch size distribution. do you have a starter JSON?
[05:03] Samir: yes, I'll share a starter Grafana dashboard json. it uses OTEL metrics and includes alert rules for drop in kv_hit_ratio below threshold and p99 latency spike.
[05:11] Ivy: note about metrics names: we use redwood.runtime.request_latency_ms, redwood.runtime.token_latency_ms, redwood.runtime.kv_cache_hit_ratio, redwood.runtime.avg_batch_size. map those to your prom/OTLP collector with same labels: route, model_variant, zone.
[05:27] Daniel: are these metrics dimensionality heavy — route and model_variant are fine but zone could be many values.
[05:31] Ivy: we recommend limiting zone to region only — long tail zones should be aggregated. Also you can use relabeling in collector to drop or map labels.
[05:40] Priya: on the OTEL collector placement question — you mentioned sidecar vs central. pros/cons?
[05:45] Ivy: sidecar gives per-pod isolation and minimal network hops, but increases resource cost because each runtime instance runs a collector process. central collector reduces duplication and is easier to enforce relabeling and retention, but adds one network hop and single point to scale. For Private we often deploy a central collector in the VPC with autoscaling and an internal LB.
[06:05] Marta: we prefer central collector to unify with our tracing pipeline. we also have strict retention policies; how do we purge token debug traces after 48 hours?
[06:13] Ivy: Redwood's telemetry exporter tags debug traces and you can configure retention on your collector side by filtering trace.instrumentation_library.name or resource.attribute. We'll show an example config to drop traces older than X or to delete on a schedule.
[06:26] Daniel: do you support OTel native SpanProcessor sampling + attribute-based sampling?
[06:30] Ivy: yes, attribute-based sampling is supported — you can sample on route, kv_cache_miss=true, or on a custom header. The runtime adds a request_id attribute so sampled traces are easy to join with logs.
[06:41] Samir: quick interjection — what's your wanted SLA for observability? Marta?
[06:45] Marta: we'd like <100ms added telemetry overhead for p95 and no more than 3% CPU cost on the inference node.
[06:52] Ivy: that's achievable with aggregated metrics and low sampling rate. sidecars can be tuned to batch OTLP exports and compress payloads; CPU overhead for aggregated metrics is typically <1-2%.
[07:03] Priya: for on-prem deployments where internet is banned, are there special packages?
[07:08] Samir: Redwood provides an on-prem bundle that runs everything in-customer-network including a lightweight collector config. we also ship example K8s manifests to deploy collector as a central service in a private namespace.
[07:18] Daniel: instrumentation detail — when you say token_latency_ms, what exactly is measured?
[07:21] Ivy: token_latency_ms is the time between the token being pulled from KV cache (or model compute start) and the token emission. It includes model decode time and any kernel rematerialization. For cache hits we also emit cache_lookup_ms; for misses we emit compute_ms.
[07:33] Marta: can we see a sample OTLP span payload?
[07:36] Ivy: yes, I'll paste an example in the follow-up. quick sample: request.span{request_id, route, token_count, p95_token_ms, kv_cache_hit_ratio}; sampled_token.span[numbered]{token_index, token_ms, kv_hit}.
[07:50] Daniel: we want to wire that into our existing Loki/Tempo/Prometheus stack. any gotchas?
[07:55] Ivy: make sure your collector has metric passthrough enabled for histogram->prometheus; Tempo likes traces with consistent trace_id. Also ensure your relabel rules don't drop token attributes you rely on (e.g., token_index). For Loki logs, correlate with request_id.
[08:09] Priya: about privacy — you said default scrubbing removes token surfaces. can we also hash tokens client-side so that even debug traces never contain cleartext?
[08:16] Ivy: yes, runtime can emit token_hash attributes instead of plaintext, using a customer-provided salt if required. that ensures even debug spans are pseudonymized.
[08:24] Marta: great. shifting to quantization profiling — we want to run a workload with int8 and int4 variants. what telemetry will show quality regressions versus latency improvements?
[08:33] Ivy: you'll want to compare model_quality metrics (we recommend running eval prompt-sets as part of the sim), response_consistency scores, and token-level perplexity metrics (we export approximate token_score). For latency, compare p50/p95 per-token times across model_variants and look at overall throughput.
[08:48] Daniel: how do we label those experiments in the telemetry?
[08:51] Ivy: tag requests with model_variant and experiment_id. Our rollout system can attach rollout metadata so you can filter metrics by experiment and run A/B comparisons in Grafana.
[08:59] Samir: we also support automatic rollback if a rollout causes a p99 regression above configured thresholds.
[09:05] Marta: back to dashboards — can alerts be tied to KV miss anomalies? e.g., sudden drop in hit ratio for a template?
[09:12] Ivy: yes, we recommend three alert classes: sharp drop in kv_hit_ratio (statistical anomaly), sustained increase in avg_batch_wait_ms (indicates scheduling problems), and p99 token latency regressions. We can provide alert rule examples for Prometheus/Alertmanager.
[09:27] Daniel: will you share a pre-built dashboard panel that shows per-route batch wait distribution?
[09:31] Samir: yes, included in the dashboard JSON.
[09:34] Priya: security/compliance note — audit logs for which entities changed sampling rules? we need an auditable trail.
[09:41] Ivy: configuration changes to sampling and telemetry are recorded in the control plane audit logs and can also be forwarded to your SIEM. On Private, those logs can stay in your VPC or be pushed to your inside collector.
[09:52] Marta: ok, last section: performance profiling under burst. we want a 48-hour sim to show p95/p99 under our traffic including cold-starts and spikes. what's the best way to run that?
[10:01] Ivy: two approaches: 1) Redwood SE-run: we run the sim on a staging cluster with instrumentation and share results; 2) self-run: we provide a load harness and OTEL config. For fidelity include realistic user think times and request size distribution plus some heavy-tail long-context requests. We'll run both kv-cache enabled and disabled to measure delta.
[10:20] Daniel: costs?
[10:22] Samir: SE-run is covered under our technical validation for enterprise prospects; self-run we provide a free trial staging credit for test clusters.
[10:29] Marta: perfect. any other gotchas?
[10:31] Ivy: one more — when you relabel or drop labels in the collector to control cardinality, be careful not to drop route+experiment_id pairs; otherwise you'll lose slicing for rollouts. Also watch out for high-cardinality user-id labels — use hashing or sampling.
[10:47] Samir: ok let's recap next steps. I'll send the OTEL config and dashboard JSON, Ivy will run the KV-cache sim and share logs, Marta will upload a traffic sample by Tuesday. Any other asks?
[10:58] Priya: can we get a short note on retention recommendations for debug traces?
[11:02] Ivy: yes — I'll include recommended retention settings and a collector filter to auto-delete debug traces after 48 hours.
[11:07] Daniel: one last question — does Redwood support sending metrics to multiple collectors for redundancy?
[11:11] Ivy: yes, you can configure primary and secondary exporter endpoints in the runtime; we also support batch buffering so if the primary is down you'll have short-term buffering to the secondary.
[11:21] Marta: thanks everyone. good session.
[11:24] Samir: thanks — we'll follow up with artifacts. meeting adjourned.
